title: Salesforce Flips the AI Script: From AI's Lunch to Its Growth Engine
subtitle: The company Wall Street said AI would kill just posted a record quarter, launched Claudeforce with Anthropic, and watched its stock rocket roughly 20%.
summary: Record Q2, $1.5B Agentforce ARR, and Claudeforce — Salesforce's rebuttal to the 'SaaSpocalypse' sent shares soaring.

bodyHtml:
Salesforce is the world's #1 CRM — customer relationship management software, the system businesses use to track every customer, every lead, every deal, and every support ticket in one place. For two decades it's been the default operating system for sales and service teams. Now it's betting that AI agents — autonomous digital workers that act on a company's behalf — become the next layer.

That bet just paid off in spectacular fashion. Salesforce reported record fiscal Q2 results after Wednesday's close, and by Thursday the stock was rocketing roughly 20% — one of the best days in the company's history. The reason isn't just the numbers, though. It's the story those numbers tell: enterprise software isn't the victim of AI. It's the distribution channel.

For two years, Wall Street priced Salesforce like a dinosaur waiting for the asteroid. Every new frontier-model launch was treated as another nail in the software coffin — the "SaaSpocalypse," as CEO Marc Benioff calls it. Customers wouldn't need clunky apps anymore, the theory went. They'd just tell an AI what they wanted and watch it happen.

This quarter is the rebuttal. Revenue hit a record $11.35 billion, up 11% year over year, with GAAP earnings per share of $4.29 — up 119%. But the number that matters most isn't in the income statement. AI didn't replace the software. AI became the software. And the growth is accelerating, not decelerating — the exact opposite of the doom loop the bears had priced in.

Meet Agentforce, Salesforce's AI-agent platform. It's the product that lets companies deploy digital workers on top of their existing CRM data — agents that follow up on leads, answer support tickets, and close deals while humans sleep. The traction is stunning: Agentforce's annual recurring revenue just blew past $1.5 billion, and combined with Data Cloud it's running at nearly $3.9 billion ARR, up more than 210% year over year.

Two years ago that number was roughly zero. Today it's a real business with real customers, sitting on top of the data Salesforce has been collecting for twenty years. That's the moat, and it's getting wider.

And then there's the big one: Claudeforce. Salesforce is putting its entire CRM inside Anthropic's Claude, an expanded partnership that plugs the hottest frontier model directly into the workflows millions of sales teams already use. That's not a concession to AI. That's a power move.

Think about what Salesforce actually owns. It has the customer data, the workflows, and the relationships — the messy, human, real-world stuff no model can conjure from thin air. Claude is the brain. Salesforce is the nervous system. And no matter who wins the model wars, the companies that own the customer relationship still get paid.

The rest of the quarter reads like a trophy case. Current remaining performance obligations — the bookings already signed — hit $33.5 billion, accelerating to 14% growth in constant currency, with total RPO at $66.3 billion. Net income rose 87% to roughly $3.53 billion, boosted by a $2.6 billion gain on Salesforce's Anthropic stake. Full-year guidance went up, and Q3 is pegged at $11.42 billion to $11.50 billion in revenue with adjusted EPS of $3.42 to $3.44.

Wall Street's verdict was unambiguous: a roughly 20% pop, one of its best sessions ever. For a company the market had written off as AI's lunch, that's not a bounce. That's a repricing.

Here's the bottom line. The SaaSpocalypse never happened, and this quarter is the proof. The companies that sit between the models and the customers are the ones that win — because they're the ones who know what you want to buy before you do. Salesforce just showed the whole market how that game is played. The dinosaurs, it turns out, were the ones holding the meteor.
